episode_title: The Hidden Cost of Endless Alignment Loops with Jyoti Pandey (Senior Director, Global Finance Data Strategy Leader, Eli Lilly)

real_qa.q: Why do organizations fall into endless alignment loops before taking action?
real_qa.r: Over-alignment happens because it feels like progress—you're in a room with smart people, debating important things, building slides, and it has all the texture of movement, but nothing is really moving. The deeper reason is that over-alignment is really about thoroughness and fear wearing a professional outfit. People add one more stakeholder, one more review cycle, one more version of the deck because nobody wants to be the person who moved too fast, and the calendar fills up with work that doesn't actually advance the initiative.
real_qa.requete: why alignment loops keep organizations stuck

real_qa.q: What are the visible and invisible costs of endless alignment loops in organizations?
real_qa.r: The visible cost is time and the invisible cost is belief. When people watch initiatives disappear into alignment loops, they stop raising their hand. They start pre-apologizing for ideas they haven't even finished saying out loud, and you end up with a culture of spectators. The true erosion of trust is harder to recover from than any delayed timeline, and the lack of innovation means people simply stop coming with ideas because the process takes so long and requires alignment from everybody.
real_qa.requete: cost of alignment loops belief time

real_qa.q: How can leaders build tangible prototypes instead of waiting for perfect consensus?
real_qa.r: Pick an actual person with a real painful problem who has agreed to show up and tell you what you built is worth anything—that person becomes your compass. Build a prototype for just five people instead of trying to get consensus across the whole organization. Those five people become chain champions who will tell everyone else that they saw something working. Word of mouth then creates a pull approach where people come asking for access rather than you pushing the initiative forward.

real_qa.q: How did Eli Lilly's data initiative shift from skepticism to momentum through a quiet product launch?
real_qa.r: After many years of workshops, pilots, and steering committees with nothing delivered, Jyoti launched the first product to a small group quietly, without fanfare, because they hadn't earned it yet. Within two weeks, she started getting messages from people she had never met saying they'd heard she'd built something cool and wanted access. Nobody sent a memo—the word just spread. That momentum after years of talking was what actually moved the room and turned skeptics into people chasing her down for access.
real_qa.requete: Eli Lilly quiet product launch momentum skeptics

real_qa.q: What is the relationship between momentum and alignment in driving transformation?
real_qa.r: Momentum creates alignment, not the other way around. Nobody rallies around a deck—they rally around evidence. You can build the most compelling case imaginable with great narrative, solid data, and senior sponsorship, and still get polite nodding. But put something that works in front of people and the conversation changes. You go from convincing to being chased. Momentum recruits people; a deck just asks them to imagine.

guest.titre: Senior Director, Global Finance Data Strategy Leader
guest.bio_context: Jyoti Pandey was hired specifically to solve a data problem at Eli Lilly that the organization had been attempting to address for many years without success. She inherited a situation full of scars from previous failed attempts—many years of workshops, pilots, and steering committees with genuine effort but no tangible results. Her mandate was to break the cycle of continuous alignment loops and make the case that building a foundation was not optional, while simultaneously keeping the organization moving fast enough to matter.
